narrative:
The model’s prediction indicates an 84% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, which is a very high risk. Because law schools aim to admit students who are likely to succeed in the profession, this risk led to your application being denied.

The most influential factor was your third-year class decile. You are in the bottom decile, while accepted students typically sit around the middle of their class. This suggests that your academic performance weakened significantly in the final year, a stage that law schools view as a strong indicator of your ability to handle rigorous coursework and prepare for the bar. The next strongest influence was your LSAT score of 20, far below the average of 37 among accepted students. This points to a fundamental gap in the reasoning and reading skills the bar exam demands, and it reinforced the model’s concern. Interestingly, your first-year decile was the third most important factor, but it actually worked in your favor. At 5, you were only slightly below the accepted average of 6, which nudged the prediction toward passing, yet not nearly enough to overcome the other two risks.

Moving forward, focus on strengthening these areas. Consider dedicating a year to structured LSAT preparation and retaking the test to raise your score substantially. If your academic circumstances caused the low third-year rank, address that head-on, perhaps by completing a rigorous post-baccalaureate program or achieving a strong graduate record. Alternatively, explore law schools that value diverse experiences and offer support for nontraditional students. With deliberate improvement, you can build a stronger application and better chances on the bar itself.
